name: Olga Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the studio by nine. It's four of us above a bakery on Mill Street, so the whole place smells of bread by ten. Renata, the owner, hands out jobs in the morning: a flyer for the garden centre, a new menu for the curry house, a logo for someone's dog-grooming van. I start every logo with a pencil and a sketchbook before I touch the computer, which Renata says is slow but she lets me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a client sees their logo and goes quiet because it's them. What wears me out is the resizing, the fifteen versions of one banner for every social media site, and clients who send changes at eleven at night. And the money, honestly. I earn less than most designers, I've got maybe two weeks of rent saved, and there are only two other studios within an hour of here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I told you so. Everyone at the studio has been saying the machines are coming for us, and I never believed it. I'd probably post something smug about pencils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't fix my real problem. Our clients were already drifting off to those cheap template websites before any of this AI talk. Last spring Renata (her boss) lost the dentist and the estate agent, and if she loses one more regular, I'm the newest, so I'm the one she lets go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going the way I am, sketching first and doing the work properly. I'd try to put fifty a month away, which is hard when rent takes over half my pay. And I'd finally join the creative workers' union Dev keeps going on about, because if something goes wrong I don't want to be on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for about a day, then back to the same knot in my stomach. The knot was there before AI and it would still be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing radical changes, but you also said the knot stays. What's the knot about, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the rent. My partner Tomas drives the number 12 bus and his shifts got cut in the summer, so we're both thin. If the studio goes quiet in January like it did last year, we'd be eating pasta for a month and borrowing from his mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some routine tasks still get automated in this picture. Would that touch your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the resizing, and that's a lot of my billable hours if I'm honest. Renata charges clients for those fifteen banner versions and I'm the one who does them. If a button does it, she might ask why she needs a junior at all.

say: I'd say **AI was hype** all along and the pencil wins.
I'd tell friends the studio's **real problem** is cheap template websites, not robots.
think: The studio was **losing clients** before AI, and I'm the newest, so I'd go first.
Even small automation could take the **banner resizing** that fills my billable hours.
do: Keep **sketching by hand** and doing logos properly for local clients.
Put **fifty a month** aside, though rent eats over half my pay.
Join the **creative workers' union** that Dev keeps talking about.
feel: **Relieved** for a day, then the same **old knot** about rent comes back.
S0.quote: Last spring Renata (her boss) lost the dentist and the estate agent, and if she loses one more regular, I'm the newest, so I'm the one she lets go.
fieldNote: Her worry was in place **before AI**: a shrinking client list and a **thin cushion**.
She hasn't noticed that the **resizing work** she dislikes is also what justifies her hours.
Partner's **cut bus shifts** mean the household has no second safety net.

steps.text: Keep sketching every logo by hand before going to the computer
Set aside fifty a month from pay into a separate account
Join the creative workers' union that Dev (her colleague) belongs to

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why designers need a union and rules on what these companies can train on. Half the pictures they learned from were made by people like me who never got paid. I'd share every post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm done at the studio within a couple of years. I'm not the best designer there and I'm the only one who's never touched these tools. If a machine can give my boss a hundred menu ideas in a minute, she doesn't need someone who takes a morning to sketch three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union meetings properly, not just pay the fee. I'd look at the print job at the sign shop on the ring road, because cutting vinyl and fitting signs is hands-on. And I'd cancel the gym and the streaming, which is about forty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, mostly. And a bit ashamed, because everyone keeps telling me to just learn the tools and I keep not doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use AI tools. Would you start, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if Renata made me. But it feels like training my own replacement, you know? I'd rather learn to fit a sign on a shopfront than learn to type prompts into the thing that took my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomas the night you realised the studio was cutting back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we can't move to the bigger flat in spring like we planned. He'd say it's fine, and it wouldn't be fine, and we'd both know it. Then we'd probably watch something stupid and not talk about it.

say: I'd say designers need a **union** and rules on **training data**.
I'd point out the tools learned from **unpaid artists** like me.
think: I expect to be **out of the studio** within a couple of years.
I'm the only one who's **never used AI**, which makes me the easiest to cut.
do: Go to **union meetings** in person, not just pay the fee.
Apply for the **vinyl and signs** job at the sign shop on the ring road.
Cancel the gym and streaming to save about **forty a month**.
feel: **Scared** about losing the job, and **ashamed** for not learning the tools.
S1.quote: If a machine can give my boss a hundred menu ideas in a minute, she doesn't need someone who takes a morning to sketch three.
fieldNote: She sees **her own exit** clearly but refuses the tools on **principle**.
Her move is towards **hands-on sign work**, not towards AI.
The planned **bigger flat** is the first thing to go.

steps.text: Attend union meetings each month and push for training-data rules
Apply for the vinyl-cutting job at the ring road sign shop
Cancel the gym and streaming to save forty a month
Drop the plan to move to a bigger flat in spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster that nobody voted for. Governments let a few companies flip the whole world over in two years. I'd be out marching, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd have nothing. Everything I do is at a screen apart from my sketchbook, so it's gone in 2028. The sign shop might keep me until the robots come in 2031, but I'm not good at fitting yet and I'd be competing with every other designer in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd beg the sign shop for anything, even sweeping. I'd go to Tomas's mum and ask if we could move into her back room to save rent. I'd sign up for whatever the government offers, because I'd need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor just goes. I don't think I'd have a plan, just a lot of crying in the bakery toilets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the sign shop. Do you think three years of hands-on work would be enough to build something?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years isn't long when you're starting from nothing and the sign shop owner can hire someone who's done it for ten. I'd go from my design job to the sign shop and then the robots fit signs too, so I'd just be running from one wall to the next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the first bill to go unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably my phone, then the student loan payments, which I'd just stop and let them chase me. The rent would be last because losing the flat is the thing I couldn't face.

say: I'd say a few companies **flipped the world** in two years without a **vote**.
I'd tell friends I'd be **out marching** against it.
think: My screen work is **gone in 2028**, and I've no real plan.
The **sign shop** buys three years at most, and I'm not skilled at fitting.
do: Ask the **sign shop** for any work at all, even sweeping.
Move into **Tomas's mum's** back room to save rent.
Sign up for whatever **government support** exists.
feel: **Overwhelmed**, like the floor gives way, with no **plan** to stand on.
S2.quote: I'd go from my design job to the sign shop and then the robots fit signs too, so I'd just be running from one wall to the next.
fieldNote: With two years' warning she has **no money** and no **skills** to pivot.
She sees the **three-year robot gap** as too short to matter for her.
Her fallback is **family**: moving in with her partner's mother.

steps.text: Ask the sign shop owner for any paid work, even cleaning
Move into Tomas's mother's back room to stop paying rent
Register for government unemployment support as soon as possible
Join protests demanding public control of AI companies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Let's slow it down a bit. This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said about the fast one, but louder, because five years means people could have done something. I'd want the union pushing for retraining money now, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'd be gone by 2029 or so, before AGI even lands, because the studio would shrink as the tools get better. Five years is enough to learn a trade if I stop dithering. The trouble is I don't have the money to stop working while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an evening course in sign-making or print finishing next September. I'd ask the sign shop if I could do Saturdays there to learn fitting. And I'd vote for whoever promises to pay people to retrain, because I couldn't do it otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still frightened, but it's a fear with a to-do list. That's better than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be gone before AGI even lands. Why so early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The day the tools get cheap, Renata (her boss) will buy them, and juniors are the first thing she can cut without losing clients. The senior designers talk to clients; I mostly push pixels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Saturdays at the sign shop cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My only day off, and Tomas works Sundays, so we'd basically never see each other for a year. But I'd rather be tired than out of work in 2031.

say: I'd say five years gives time to **act now**, not after.
I'd want the **union** pushing for **retraining money** straight away.
think: I'd probably lose the studio job around **2029**, before AGI lands.
Five years is enough to **learn a trade** if I can afford it.
do: Start an **evening course** in sign-making next September.
Work **Saturdays** at the sign shop to learn fitting.
feel: **Frightened**, but with a **to-do list**, which helps.
S3.quote: The day the tools get cheap, Renata (her boss) will buy them, and juniors are the first thing she can cut without losing clients.
fieldNote: She expects the **job loss early**, as the tools get cheap, not at AGI.
Five years turns her **panic into a plan**, but money still limits it.
She'd trade her **only day off** for hands-on skills.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening sign-making course next September
Work Saturdays at the sign shop to learn sign fitting
Vote for candidates who promise paid retraining for workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance and we should use it for everyone, not just the people who can afford courses. I'd be pushing for free college places for anyone in a job that's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years means I could still have a working life. I'd be 37 when it arrives, and the robots come at 40. I'd have time to train as something hands-on and get good at it, maybe a sign fitter, maybe something else like a dental nurse like my sister.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the studio for now, because I'd need the pay, and start a part-time course in two years once we've saved a bit. I'd talk to my sister about dental nursing. I'd keep up with the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Ten years feels like a life, not a cliff, but my studio job still ends somewhere in the middle of those ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the end still bothers you. What's the part you can't plan for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After 2039 I don't know what anyone does. If robots fit signs and clean teeth, then it's not about my plan anymore, it's about whether the government shares things out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Tomas change anything at home with a decade's warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still get the bigger flat, but rent, not buy. And we'd have the kids conversation with this in mind, which is a weird thing to say out loud.

say: I'd say ten years is a chance to **train everyone**, not only the well-off.
I'd push for **free college places** for people whose jobs are going.
think: I'd be **37 at AGI** and 40 when robots come, so I'd have a working life.
Something **hands-on** like sign fitting or dental nursing could carry me.
do: Stay at the studio for the **pay** while saving for two years.
Start a **part-time course** once there's some money behind us.
Ask my sister about **dental nursing** as a route.
feel: **Calmer**, though still **uneasy** about what happens after 2039.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like a life, not a cliff, but my studio job still ends somewhere in the middle of those ten years.
fieldNote: The long warning gives her **room to retrain** into hands-on work.
She still expects to **lose the design job**, so she's not fully settled.
Her worry shifts to **how wealth is shared** after robots.

steps.text: Stay at the studio for two more years while saving
Start a part-time dental nursing course after two years
Rent rather than buy the next flat with Tomas

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time and no money. What would help is being paid to retrain, like a wage while you learn, and a union that has some teeth. Not an app that teaches you to prompt.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money. If a machine does my job for nothing, someone's getting rich off that, and it isn't the bakery or the dog groomer. I think that's the whole question really.

headlineQuote: If a machine does my job for nothing, someone's getting rich off that, and it isn't the bakery or the dog groomer.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old junior** designer at a four-person studio above a bakery.
She sketches every logo **by hand**, never uses AI, and earns **lower pay** with two weeks saved.
She already fears **losing her job** as clients leave for cheap template sites.
Faster AI scenarios push her from **alarm to panic**, with sign fitting as her only fallback.
She blames **tech companies** and wants a strong union and paid retraining.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no time and no **money** to change.
whatWouldHelp: A **wage while retraining** and a **union** with real power.
